concept: Read concern and causal consistency with secondary reads

claims.text: Read preference selects eligible replica-set members; directing reads to secondaries can return stale data because replication from the primary is asynchronous. (high confidence)

For durable causal consistency, execute dependent operations in a causally consistent client session with majority read concern and majority write concern. This combination guarantees read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, and writes-follow-reads, including when reads use secondaries. (high confidence)
A causally consistent read cannot depend on an unacknowledged w:0 write because the session receives no operation time for that write. (high confidence)

MongoDB 8.0 changed majority-write acknowledgment to follow oplog persistence rather than completion of secondary application. An immediate secondary read outside a causally consistent session can therefore miss the acknowledged update. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Majority read concern uses a committed timestamped snapshot rather than polling every replica for the latest value. Without an additional causal-time requirement it usually need not wait for new writes, although snapshot availability and replication lag can cause blocking. (low confidence)
Majority read concern alone does not mean reading the latest primary state: it can return an older majority-committed snapshot on the selected member. (high confidence)

A majority write followed in the same causal session by a majority read with secondary read preference reflects the preceding write; if the selected secondary has not reached the dependency time, the read waits. (high confidence)

Drivers track operationTime in the client session and send it as readConcern.afterClusterTime on subsequent supported causally consistent commands. They also gossip clusterTime; applications should use the session API to carry this causal context. (high confidence)

Applications must serialize operations within a client session. To preserve dependencies across sessions, explicitly advance the receiving session operation time and cluster time from the originating session. (high confidence)

Causal consistency does not isolate a session from concurrent outside writes. A subsequent read may include intervening writes, so these guarantees should not be treated as snapshot isolation or a guarantee of the latest unrelated write. (medium confidence)

Do not assume that enabling causal sessions makes weaker concern settings durable: MongoDB documents partial guarantees for weaker combinations, and Jepsen historically found that causal sessions with weaker read/write concerns could violate expected causal behavior. (high confidence)

Independent Internetware research tested MongoDB 4.2.3 using formal CC, CCv, and CM checking and reported preliminary results supporting the majority-read/majority-write requirements under faults; this is historical test evidence, not validation of current server versions. (low confidence)

Read-containing multi-document transactions must use primary read preference; a causal session supporting secondary reads does not make a secondary eligible for such transaction reads. (low confidence)

Read preference selects eligible replica-set members; read concern controls the data a selected member may return. A secondary can lag the primary, and majority read concern alone does not guarantee the newest write is visible. (medium confidence)

A causally dependent secondary read may wait for the secondary to reach the required causal time. Causal consistency trades waiting for dependency order; it does not make asynchronous replication instantaneous. (high confidence)

Operations in different client sessions need an explicit causal handoff: advance the receiving session's operation time and cluster time from the producing session. An acknowledgment or application notification alone does not transfer that session context. (medium confidence)

Do not assume that enabling a causal session repairs weaker concerns. MongoDB documents fewer durable guarantees with local reads or w:1 writes; Jepsen's 2018 tests of MongoDB 3.6.4 found causal anomalies under sub-majority settings. Those historical tests do not establish a present-version defect. (medium confidence)
